title: WHAT DOES THE BIBLE REALLY SAY ABOUT REMARRIAGE?
paragraphs:
WHAT DOES THE BIBLE REALLY SAY ABOUT REMARRIAGE?
Before You Call Someone’s Second Marriage “Adultery,” Before You Tell a Divorced Christian They Can Never Love Again, and Before You Use Grace as Permission to Ignore Jesus—Read What Scripture Actually Says
There is a wedding ring sitting in a drawer somewhere tonight.
Not because someone stopped believing in marriage.
Not because they woke up one morning and decided covenant did not matter.
But because something they once believed would last until death… died while both people were still breathing.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you did the betraying.
Maybe you begged someone to stay.
Maybe you were the one who left.
Maybe there was adultery.
Maybe abandonment.
Maybe years of decisions you wish you could undo.
Maybe you have since remarried, and every time somebody quotes one of Jesus’ warnings about divorce, something cold moves through your chest:
Am I living in adultery right now?
Does God recognize my marriage?
Do I have to leave my present spouse to obey Jesus?
Can a divorced Christian ever marry again?
Or perhaps you are single after divorce, wondering whether wanting companionship again means you are rebelling against God.
These questions cannot be answered responsibly with a meme.
And they should never be answered by ripping one sentence from the Bible, weaponizing it against wounded people, and calling that faithfulness.
But neither can we answer them by saying, “God wants you happy,” as though happiness were the highest commandment in Scripture.
Jesus deserves something better from us.
Truth.
All of it.
Because the Bible’s teaching on remarriage is simultaneously more serious than modern culture often wants it to be…and more saturated with grace than religious shame sometimes allows it to be.
And before we talk about remarriage, we have to understand why divorce hurts so deeply in Scripture.
Jesus takes us backward.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce, He did not begin with loopholes.
He went back to creation.

“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female… Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
—Matthew 19:4–6
That last idea becomes even sharper in Greek:
ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω
ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō
In straightforward sense:
“Therefore, what God joined together, let a human being not separate.”
That word συνέζευξεν — synezeuxen carries the idea of joining or yoking together.
Jesus therefore refuses to reduce marriage to paperwork, romance, sexual attraction, financial partnership, or social convenience.
Marriage is covenantal.
Two become one flesh.
That is why biblical Christianity cannot treat divorce casually.
Jesus does not.
And neither should we.
But notice what happens next.
The Pharisees bring up Moses.
Why, then, did Moses permit a certificate of divorce?
Jesus responds that Moses permitted it because of the hardness of human hearts, “but from the beginning it was not so.”
There is something devastatingly honest there.
Divorce exists in Scripture not because broken covenant is beautiful, but because human beings are broken.
Hardness.
Sin.
Betrayal.
Rebellion.
Human hearts capable of destroying what God intended to flourish.
Then Jesus speaks the sentence that has frightened countless divorced Christians:
“Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery…”
—Matthew 19:9
The crucial Greek expression is:
μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ — mē epi porneia
“except/on account of porneia.”
The word πορνεία — porneia refers broadly to sexual immorality, though interpreters have debated the precise scope intended in Matthew’s context.
And this matters.
Jesus is demolishing the idea that someone may discard a spouse for trivial reasons and then simply replace that spouse as though covenant meant nothing.
He is defending the sacredness of marriage.
He is exposing the sinfulness of covenant-breaking.
And Matthew records an exception involving porneia.

Christians have disagreed for centuries about exactly how that exception relates to remarriage. One longstanding interpretation understands Jesus as permitting divorce and subsequent remarriage for the innocent spouse after sexual immorality. Other Christians understand the exception more narrowly or believe that even where divorce is permissible, remarriage while the former spouse lives remains prohibited.
We should be humble enough to say that disagreement exists.
But we must not be dishonest about what the text says.
Jesus gives marriage enormous moral weight.
He condemns covenant-breaking divorce.
He identifies sexual immorality as an exceptional circumstance in Matthew’s account.
And He refuses to let human beings turn marriage into something disposable.
Then Paul takes us into another painful situation.
What happens when somebody does not commit adultery but simply abandons the marriage?
In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul tells believers not to divorce an unbelieving spouse merely because that spouse does not share the faith.
If the unbelieving husband or wife is willing to remain, the Christian should not throw the marriage away.
Then comes verse 15:
“But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases…”
The Greek contains an important expression:
οὐ δεδούλωται — ou dedoulōtai
Literally, the brother or sister “has not been enslaved” or “is not bound as a slave” in such circumstances.
Paul then says:
ἐν δὲ εἰρήνῃ κέκληκεν ὑμᾶς ὁ θεός
“God has called you to peace.”
Here again, Christians who take Scripture seriously disagree about the implications.
Some understand “not bound” to mean that when an unbelieving spouse abandons the marriage, the deserted believer is released from the marriage and may eventually remarry.

Others understand Paul as permitting the separation while not necessarily granting permission for remarriage, pointing especially to his earlier instruction that a separated spouse should remain unmarried or be reconciled.
That disagreement should not be hidden.
If someone tells you that every detail of 1 Corinthians 7:15 has always been universally interpreted the same way, that overstates the evidence.
But Scripture gives us something that is not disputed.
A believer is not commanded to force an abandoning unbeliever to remain.
“Let him depart.”
God has called His people to peace.
Then there is one circumstance where Scripture is unmistakably explicit about freedom to remarry:
death.
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 7:39
The Greek is beautifully direct:
ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ᾧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι, μόνον ἐν κυρίῳ
eleuthera estin hō thelei gamēthēnai, monon en Kyriō
“She is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”
Death ends the marriage covenant.
Remarriage after widowhood is therefore clearly permitted.
But perhaps that is not why you clicked this article.
Perhaps your history is messier.
You did not lose your spouse to death.
You lost your marriage to sin.
Maybe even your own sin.
And this is where theological discussion becomes painfully personal.
Because there is another question hiding underneath “Can I remarry?”
It is:
“What does Jesus do with someone who has already ruined everything?”
Now we have reached the Gospel.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally the announcement that morally successful people get to keep their spotless records.
Christianity announces that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
That includes sexual sinners.
Adulterers.
The sexually immoral.
The selfish.
The deceptive.
The proud.
The people who destroyed things they should have protected.
Paul gives a terrifying list in 1 Corinthians 6 and says that the sexually immoral and adulterers will not inherit the kingdom of God.
But he does not stop there.
“And such were some of you…”
καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε — kai tauta tines ēte
“Such were some of you.”
Were.
Then comes grace:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus…”
That is Christianity.
Not pretending sin never happened.
Not renaming adultery “finding yourself.”
Not baptizing selfishness with therapeutic vocabulary.
Not calling evil good.
But neither is Christianity telling the repentant sinner:
“You did something terrible, therefore terrible is what you will always be.”
Jesus Christ does something human beings cannot do.
He forgives guilty people without pretending they were innocent.
At the cross, grace does not deny the scandal.
Grace answers it.
Maybe you destroyed your first marriage.
Then repent.
Not performatively.
Not, “I made mistakes.”
Call sin what God calls it.
Confess it.
Where restitution or reconciliation is biblically possible and appropriate, pursue what obedience requires.
Ask forgiveness where you have sinned against people.
Stop blaming everybody else.
Bring the ugly truth into the light.
Because repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the grave.
The Greek word so often associated with repentance is μετάνοια — metanoia: a turning, a change of mind that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying people.
Grace transforms.
But what if you have already remarried?
What if children now call both of you Mom and Dad?
What if years have passed?
Should you divorce your current spouse to somehow undo the first divorce?
Scripture nowhere establishes a general command for Christians in an existing remarriage to dissolve that marriage as an act of repentance.
That would attempt to repair one broken covenant by breaking another.

Whatever sins may have surrounded the road into a present marriage should be confessed before God. But repentance now means faithfulness to Christ in the life actually before you—not pretending you possess a time machine.
If you are married now, honor your covenant now.
Love sacrificially now.
Become trustworthy now.
Be sexually faithful now.
Forgive now.
Pray together now.
Put Christ at the center now.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem what yesterday did to you.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
David was forgiven, yet consequences remained.
Peter was restored, yet he still remembered the courtyard.
Grace does not mean history becomes imaginary.
Grace means history no longer gets the final word.
And that is why remarriage cannot be discussed faithfully without talking about redemption.
Some people reading this need permission to stop treating marriage casually.
Others need permission to stop treating themselves as permanently contaminated.
Some need conviction.
Some need comfort.
Some need to fight for the marriage they still have instead of fantasizing about another one.
Some need to repent of adultery.
Some need to forgive someone who abandoned them.
Some need wise pastoral counsel before entering another marriage.
Some need to stop allowing loneliness to make theological decisions for them.
And some remarried believers need to stop waking up every morning wondering whether Jesus secretly despises their family.
Listen carefully.
Your marital history is not your Savior.
Your perfect record would not have saved you.
Your broken record cannot save you.
Jesus saves sinners.
This is why Romans 8:1 remains breathtaking:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα
Ouden ara nyn katakrima.
“Therefore, now, no condemnation…”
Not less condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
Not condemnation waiting behind the church door whenever someone discovers your history.
For those who are genuinely in Christ, there is no condemnation before God because Christ bore judgment for His people.
That grace should never make us casual about marriage.
It should make us more serious about marriage.
The person forgiven of covenant-breaking should understand covenant differently.
The adulterer who has truly encountered Christ should become fiercely faithful.
The liar should become truthful.
The selfish spouse should learn sacrifice.
The wounded spouse should discover that forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
The divorced believer should discover that “divorced” is a description of something that happened, not the name Jesus carved over their soul.
And anyone considering remarriage should slow down long enough to ask questions much deeper than:
“Do I deserve another chance?”
Ask:
“Will this marriage glorify Jesus Christ?”
“Have I genuinely repented of my contribution to the destruction of my previous marriage?”
“Am I entering this relationship from spiritual health or simply terror of being alone?”
“Have I sought mature biblical counsel?”
“Is this person truly following Christ?”
“Are there unresolved covenant obligations I am trying to escape?”
“Am I willing to make this marriage a testimony of Christlike faithfulness rather than another attempt to medicate my loneliness?”
Because biblical remarriage is not about getting another wedding.
It is about covenant.
And sometimes the most Christlike answer is not rushing toward another relationship.
Sometimes God needs to heal things in you that another person cannot heal.
Sometimes loneliness reveals idols.
Sometimes silence reveals wounds.
Sometimes singleness becomes the room where Jesus teaches you that being wanted romantically and being loved eternally are not the same thing.
Do not ask another human being to become your resurrection.
They cannot carry that weight.
Christ can.
And please hear this too:

If you are currently trapped in violence, coercion, credible threats, or serious abuse, do not interpret a discussion about the sanctity of marriage as a command to remain physically exposed to danger. Seek immediate safety, appropriate authorities where necessary, mature pastoral care, and qualified professional help. Christians differ on how abuse relates specifically to biblical grounds for divorce and remarriage, but protecting someone from immediate harm is not the same thing as treating marriage casually.
The church must be capable of saying two things at once:
Marriage is sacred.
And:
Broken people are not disposable.
We can defend covenant without crushing survivors.
We can preach repentance without withholding grace.
We can tell adulterers to repent without pretending adulterers are beyond redemption.
We can tell abandoned people that God sees them without automatically answering every complicated remarriage case with a slogan.
We can honor Jesus enough to refuse both extremes.
Because Jesus did not come to make sin irrelevant.
He came because sin was so deadly that nothing less than His blood could rescue us.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needs tonight.
Your divorce may be part of your story.
Your adultery may be part of your story.
Your abandonment may be part of your story.
Your courtroom may be part of your story.
Your shattered wedding vows may be part of your story.
Your lonely apartment may be part of your story.
Your second marriage may be part of your story.
But none of those things deserve the throne.
Jesus does.
From scandal…
to grace.
Not because the scandal was insignificant.
Because the Savior is greater.
Bring it to Jesus.
If you need repentance, repent.
If you need forgiveness, ask.
If you owe someone an apology, stop rehearsing excuses.
If your marriage is barely breathing, seek godly help before pride signs the death certificate.
If you are divorced and ashamed, stop assuming the whispers of religious people carry more authority than the Gospel.
If you are remarried, do not spend the rest of your marriage staring backward when Christ is calling you to faithfulness today.
And if you are wondering whether grace could possibly reach the particular wreckage carrying your name…
Look at the cross.
That is where Christianity answers scandal.
Not with denial.
With blood.
Not with excuses.
With atonement.
Not with “you were never guilty.”
With something infinitely better:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.”
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Not because every difficult question can be settled by one article, but because shame has a way of making us forget what grace taught us yesterday.
You need Jesus.
Not merely another marriage.
Not merely a restored reputation.
Not merely another chance at romance.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Christ.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who tells the truth about our sin and then bears the judgment sinners could never bear themselves.
The One who can take a chapter you wish had never been written and refuse to let it become the ending.
Because perhaps the greatest question is not:
“Can I marry again?”
Perhaps the question beneath it is:
“Can Jesus still make something holy out of a life that has been broken?”
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at Peter after denial.
Look at Paul after persecution.
Look at the countless sinners Scripture refuses to airbrush.
Then remember:
The Gospel has never been the story of flawless people presenting God with flawless histories.
It is the story of a flawless Savior rescuing people who desperately need grace.
And maybe your wedding ring is still sitting in that drawer.
Maybe another one is already on your hand.
Maybe there will never be another ring.
But your deepest hope was never supposed to fit around your finger.
Your deepest hope has nail scars in His hands.
Your past may explain the scars—but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
